rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: God formed humans unlike beasts and beasts unlike humans, giving every creature its measured creation.
rows.anchor: ما قاله مجاهد وهو أنه قال: (لم يجعل خلق الإنسان كخلق البهائم، ولا خلق البهائم كخلق الإنسان

rows.speaker: عطية، ومقاتل
rows.claim: They take ‘gave each thing its creation’ to mean that God gave it its form, each animal kind having a distinct form.
rows.anchor: قال عطية، ومقاتل: ({أعطى كل شيء خلقه} يعني صورته)

rows.speaker: الحسن، وقتادة
rows.claim: They interpret the phrase as giving each thing its fitness and what makes it sound; its form suits its purpose.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن، وقتادة: (أعطى كل شيء صلاحه وما يصلحه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this interpretation, God gave each thing the form that suits what it was created to do, then guided it to its livelihood, food, mate, and other needs.
rows.anchor: هداه لما يصلحه من معيشته ومشربه ومنكحه إلى غير ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq prefers that God created each thing in the form most useful and fitting for it, then guided it to its livelihood.
rows.anchor: اختيار أبي إسحاق وبينه فقال: (معناه: خلق كل شيء على الهيئة التي بها ينتفع

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas glosses the phrase as God perfecting everything He created.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (يريد أتقن كل ما خلق)

rows.speaker: الكلبي، والسدي
rows.claim: Their second interpretation is that God paired each creature with a mate of its own kind, such as man with woman and camel with she-camel.
rows.anchor: قول الكلبي، والسدي قالا: (أعطى الرجل المرأة، والبعير الناقة، والذكر الأنثى من جنسه)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says God guided the male to intercourse with the female of its kind.
rows.anchor: صرح السدي بهذا اللفظ قال: (أعطى الذكر الأنثى مثل خلقه (ثم هدى) قال: إلى الجماع)

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba chooses the interpretation that God pairs males and females and guides them to mating.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول اختيار ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains that God gives each male a female of its kind and inspires the male to approach the mate.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (أعطى الذكر من الناس امرأة مثله من صنفه، والشاة شاة، والثور بقرة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq accepts the mating interpretation because animals mate without having learned it; the broader interpretation of guidance to their welfare also includes this instinct.
rows.anchor: وهذا التفسير جائز؛ لأنا نرى الذكر من الحيوان يأتي الأنثى، ولم يرى ذكرا قد أتى أنثى قبله

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads ‘creation’ as created faculties: hands grasp, feet walk, tongues speak, eyes see, and ears hear.
rows.anchor: روي عن الضحاك قول آخر في {أعطى كل شيء خلقه} قال: (يعني اليد: البطش، والرجل: المشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On al-Dahhak’s reading, ‘creation’ means what is created: God placed each faculty and its benefit in the relevant bodily organ.
rows.anchor: والخلق في هذا القول في معنى المخلوق، والبطش والمشي والنظر وهذه المعاني كلها مخلوق لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ answer establishes against Pharaoh that creation and guidance require a creator and guide, who is the Lord, and no other lord exists; this supports following God’s religion and guidance.
rows.anchor: ثبت خلق وهداية لا خلاف، ولابد لهما من خالق وهاد، ذلك الخالق والهادي هو الرب، لا رب غيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes Pharaoh’s question to ask about the condition or fate of the generations that passed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد ما حال القرون التي مضت)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ‘bal’ means condition or affair; Pharaoh alludes to earlier peoples who worshipped idols rather than believing in Moses’ message, including Noah’s, ʿAd’s, and Thamud’s peoples.
rows.anchor: ومعنى البال هاهنا: الحال والشأن

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says the generations’ deeds are preserved with God, who will repay them for them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أي أعمالهم محفوظة عند الله يجازي بها)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the book as the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (اللوح المحفوظ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their deeds are written down, so they receive the recompense for what they did, just as Moses’ hearers will be judged for their own deeds; the verse links this to 2:134.
rows.anchor: أعمالهم مكتوبة مثبتة. ومعنى هذا الجواب أنهم يجازون بما عملوا، وأنت تجازى بما تعمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘My Lord neither errs nor forgets’ confirms certain recompense: He does not leave an unbeliever unpunished or forget a monotheist’s reward.
rows.anchor: تأكيد وتحقيق للجزاء بالأعمال. قال: يريد لا يترك من كفر به حتى ينتقم منه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says God does not err or forget any of their affairs, but gives good for good and evil for evil.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (لا يخطئ ربي ولا ينسى ما كان من أمرهم، حتى يوافيهم بأعمالهم بالحسن حسنا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra distinguishes losing a movable thing, such as an escaped animal, from missing the location of a fixed thing; the latter is called ḍalaltuhu, not aḍlaltuhu.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (يقال أضللت الشيء: إذا ضاع منك مثل: الدابة وما أشبهها إذا انفلت منك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says ḍalaltu a thing is to put it somewhere and not know where it is, while aḍlaltuhu is to lose it.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (ضللت الشيء أضله إذا جعلته في مكان لم تدر أين هو، وأضللته أضعته)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq allows the pronoun to refer either to the book—God does not let it go astray or forget it—or to the generations, which He does not lose or forget.
rows.anchor: لا يضله ربي ولا ينساه، يعني به الكتاب، ويجوز لا يضلها ولا ينساها، يعني به القرون

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The author takes al-Farra’s sense to mean that God does not make an error.
rows.anchor: والمعنى على ما ذكر الفراء: لا يخطئ ربي كما ذكره الكلبي

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: On Abu Ishaq’s lexical analysis, ‘does not err’ means ‘does not forget’; Mujahid likewise treats the two clauses as equivalent.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما ذكر أبو إسحاق معنى يضل: ينسى. وقد قال مجاهد: (يضل ربي ولا ينسى هما شيء واحد)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi glosses the phrase as God neither overlooking nor leaving anything.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (لا يغفل ولا يترك شيئا)

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr distinguishes a tethered camel that cannot find its place from a loose camel that wanders away, and distinguishes the agent who loses something from the object that goes missing; he derives loss from disappearance.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو: (يقال أضللت بعيري: إذا كان معقولا فلم يهتد لمكانه، وأضللته إضلالا: إذا كان مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that God is absent from nothing and nothing is absent from Him.
rows.anchor: أي: لا يغيب عن شيء ولا يغيب عنه شيء

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Reporting Muqatil, Ibn al-Anbari says Pharaoh had heard the believer’s warning about earlier nations and wanted to know their histories; Moses then lacked that knowledge because he learned their stories from the Torah, which came only after Pharaoh drowned.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: (مذهب مقاتل في هذه الآية: أن عدو الله فرعون كان قد قال له مؤمن آل فرعون

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari rejects the earlier gloss that God does not let the book go astray from Him, arguing that Arabic does not permit dropping the preposition here, as in saying ‘the dirham fell your sleeve’ for ‘from your sleeve.’
rows.anchor: وذهب الأولون إلى أن المعنى في: {لا يضل ربي} لا يضل الكتاب من ربي. قال وهذا باطل

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali explains mahd as a verbal noun like farsh, mihād as something spread like a bed or carpet, and allows mahd to be used as a noun or as ‘having a cradle’; he considers the first analysis clearer.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (المهد مصدر كالفرش، والمهاد مثل الفراش والبساط، وهما اسم ما يفرش ويبسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: S-l-k means inserting one thing into another; God laid paths in the earth for people to travel, as in the cited verse about being put into Hell and the example of a spear entering a wounded person.
rows.anchor: السلك: إدخال الشيء في الشيء يسلكه فيه قال الله تعالى: {ما سلككم في سقر}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God made paths in the earth easy for people.
rows.anchor: كما قال ابن عباس: (سهل لكم فيها طرقا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the paths stretch across and appear on the earth, the verse describes them as if they were inserted into it, by analogy with something inserted into another thing.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت الطرق المسلوكة ممتدة على الأرض ظاهرة عليها جعلت كأنها مسلوكة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water sent down from heaven is rain.
rows.anchor: {وأنزل من السماء ماء} يعني: المطر

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The نظم scholar says Moses’ reported speech ends at ‘water’; God then speaks in the first person at ‘We brought forth,’ as the following command to eat and graze indicates.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب النظم: (تم الإخبار والحكاية عن موسى عند قوله: {ماء} ثم أخبر الله تعالى عن نفسه

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: An alternative reading attaches the whole clause to Moses: God sent rain, and the human community cultivated plants with it; without rain they would not grow, as 56:63 also attributes cultivation to people.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن معناه مضاف إلى موسى على تأويل: الذي أنزل من السماء ماء فأخرجنا نحن معاشر عباده

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the plants as different kinds or varieties.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد أصنافا من النبات مختلفة)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the varieties differ in color—white, red, green, or yellow—with each color itself a kind.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: ({شتى} مختلفا ألوانه أبيض وأحمر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the plants vary in colors and tastes, and explains zawj as a color and azwāj as colors.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: ({شتى} مختلف الألوان والطعوم)

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿsha’s line uses zawj for a kind or color of brocade, supporting the gloss ‘color.’
rows.anchor: قال الأعشى (¬3): وكل زوج من الديباج يلبسه ... أبو قدامة محبوا بذاك معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shattā means varied and dispersed, has no singular in the same form, and derives from shatta, ‘to scatter’; the author lists its related verb forms.
rows.anchor: {شتى} معناه: مختلف متفرق، ولا واحد له من لفظه، مثل: فوضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shattā can modify azwāj, meaning different colors, or modify nabāt; both constructions are possible.
rows.anchor: و {شتى} في هذه الآية نعت للأزواج؛ لأن المراد ألوان مختلفة، ويجوز أن يكون من نبات

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash considers both grammatical constructions sound.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: (كل ذلك مستقيم)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari notes that nabāt is collective and has no ordinary singular, like shattā; treating the words as shatīt and nabāta would make their agreement clear, while ‘different varieties of plants’ is also sound.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن الأنباري القولين فقال: (النبات يقع على جمع لا ينفرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Eat and graze’ refers to the plants produced by the rain.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {كلوا وارعوا} أي: مما أخرجنا بالمطر من النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flock itself grazes the pasture; its owner tends it by letting it graze, turning it out, and bringing it back.
rows.anchor: يقال: رعت الماشية الكلأ رعيا، ورعاها صاحبها رعاية، إذا أسامها وسرحها وأراحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command permits grazing livestock in the rain-grown pasture and reminds people of God’s blessing.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أسيموا مواشيكم فيما أنبتناه بالمطر، وهذا أمر إباحة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas connects this reminder to 80:27–32, where God grows grain and other provisions for people and livestock.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هذا كقوله: {فأنبتنا فيها حبا} -إلى قوله- {متاعا لكم ولأنعامكم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs in the rain and plants point to God’s oneness.
rows.anchor: معنى ما ذكر من الدلالة على توحيده

rows.speaker: اللحياني
rows.claim: Al-Lihyani says nuhā means intellect and derives the name from the mind stopping at what it is commanded and not overstepping.
rows.anchor: قال اللحياني: (النهية: العقل، والنهى جمع نهيه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says a person of nuhya has reason that restrains vice and leads to good, or follows the judgment of reason; he considers the latter explanation better.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (يقال: فلان ذو نهية، ومعناه ذو عقل ينتهي به عن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two etymologies converge: intellect restrains a person from reprehensible acts.
rows.anchor: وقد رجع القولان في اشتقاق النهية إلى قول واحد، وهو الحبس، والنهية هي التي تنهي وتحبس عن المقابح

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali says nuhā may be a verbal noun like hudā or a plural like ẓulum; the plural reading is supported by its addition to ‘possessors,’ though a singular verbal noun can stand for a plural.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (لا يخلو النهى من أن يكون مصدرا كالهدى، أو جمعا كالظلم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali derives nuhā from restraint or confinement, like a place where water is held; the author says this too returns to the mind’s restraining function.
rows.anchor: والنهى معناه في اللغة: الثبات والحبس، ومنه النهى والتنهية للمكان الذي ينتهي إليه الماء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s narration, Ibn Abbas says the signs are a lesson for people of understanding who restrain themselves from disobeying God; al-Dahhak gives a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: ({لآيات لأولي النهى} يريد العبرة لذوي العقول)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s narration, Ibn Abbas glosses ‘possessors of insight’ as the pious.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الوالبي: (لذوي التقى)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God recalls His favor to Israel: He rescued them from Pharaoh, whom He drowned before their eyes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (ثم ذكر الله تعالى منته على بني إسرائيل فقال: {بني إسرائيل قد أنجيناكم من عدوكم} يعني فرعون أغرقه بمرآى منهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After drowning Pharaoh, God promised Moses the right side of the Mount and would give him the Torah there, explaining what Israel needed; the author links this to 2:51.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن الله تعالى وعد موسى بعد أن أغرق فرعون التأني جانب الطور الأيمن، فيؤتيه التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse has the readings wāʿadnā and waʿadnā.
rows.anchor: واختلف القراء في: واعدنا ووعدنا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats wāʿadnā as a dialectal form of waʿadnā, so its alif does not prove reciprocal action, just as forms on the istafʿala pattern need not mean requesting an action.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو الحسن الأخفش أن: (واعدنا لغة في وعدنا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers waʿadnā because it plainly describes a promise by one agent; wāʿadnā is less explicit, so the clearer reading is preferable.
rows.anchor: والقراءة بوعد أحسن؛ لأن واعد هاهنا بمعنى وعد، ويعلم من وعد أنه فعل واحد لا محالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the promise was made to Moses, Israel is addressed because the promise was for their sake.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوعد إنما كان لموسى، ولكن خوطبوا به؛ لأن الوعد كان لأجلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction elides ‘coming to the side of the Mount’; the right side is the side to Moses’ right.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: واعدناكم إتيان جانب الطور فحذف المضاف، والمراد بالأيمن الجانب الذي على يمين موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation says God promised Israel the mountain’s side so they could hear Him speak to Moses there.
rows.anchor: وقيل في التفسير: (وعدهم الله جانب الجبل ليسمعوا كلام الله -عز وجل- لموسى بحضرتهم هناك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s words ‘eat of the good things We provided’ are spoken as a reminder of blessings.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {كلوا} أي: وقلنا لهم كلوا {من طيبات ما رزقناكم} وهذا أمر يقتضي التعديد بالنعم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s narration, Ibn Abbas glosses ‘do not transgress in it’ as ‘do not do wrong.’
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي: (يقول لا تظلموا)

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil interprets the prohibition as ‘do not disobey.’
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: (ولا تعصوا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition means not becoming insolent over the blessing and thereby wronging others; another gloss says not to use God’s gifts as strength for disobedience.
rows.anchor: والمعنى لا تبطروا فيما أنعمت عليكم فتظالموا. وهذا المعنى قول من قال: (لا تتقووا بنعمي على معاصي)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says they must not deny God’s blessing in what He provided, which would make them transgressors.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (لا تجحدوا نعمة الله فيما رزقكم منه فتكونوا طاغين)

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says they must not exceed the limit with manna and quail by taking more than needed and storing it; storing any of it counts as transgression.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: (لا تتعدوا ما حد الله لكم في المن والسلوى فتتجاوزوا قدر ما يكفيكم وتدخروا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and others take fa-yaḥilla as ‘becomes due.’
rows.anchor: قاله قتادة وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both kasra and ḍamma readings are transmitted for yaḥilla and yaḥlil.
rows.anchor: وقرئ: {فيحل} {ومن يحلل} بالكسر والضم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra prefers kasra because it means ‘becomes due,’ matching the explanatory gloss of obligation rather than descent.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (والكسر أحب إلي من الضم؛ لأن الضم من الحلول بمعنى الوقوع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says kasra means ‘becomes due’ while ḍamma means ‘comes down.’
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: ({فيحل عليكم} معناه فيجب عليكم، ومن قرأ: بالضم، فمعناه التنزيل)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings are close in meaning: with kasra, the ban and protection lift after transgression, so punishment comes upon them; ‘becomes due’ conveys this sense rather than literally defining the word.
rows.anchor: فمعنى يحل عليكم: ينزل بكم وينالكم بعدما كان ذا حظر وحجر ومنع عنكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports kasra by 11:39 and by the kasra reading in 20:86; with ḍamma, anger is treated as the punishment that follows it and thus as something descending.
rows.anchor: {ويحل عليه عذاب مقيم} [هود: 39]، أي: ينزل به بعد أن لم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawā can mean falling from a height, an eagle swooping on prey, landing in a place, or dying; the author cites lines by al-Nābigha and Kaʿb ibn Saʿd for the sense ‘perished.’
rows.anchor: يقال: هوى يهوي هويا: إذا سقط من علو إلى أسفل

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha’s line uses hawā for Ziyad’s death or ruin.
rows.anchor: قال النابغة (¬2): وقال الشامتون هوى زياد

rows.speaker: كعب بن سعد
rows.claim: Kaʿb ibn Saʿd’s line ‘his mother perished’ illustrates hawā meaning ‘died.’
rows.anchor: قول كعب بن سعد (¬3) (¬4): هوت أمه ما يبعث الصبح غاديا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the person perished; another is that he fell into the abyss called al-Hāwiya.
rows.anchor: فأما التفسير فقيل: (هلك) (¬1). وقيل: (صار إلى الهاوية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s narration, Ibn Abbas explains ‘he has fallen’ as ‘he has become wretched.’
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي: (يقول: فقد شقي)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s and ʿAta’s reports, Ibn Abbas says repentance means turning from associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي وعطاء: (تاب من الشرك)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains faith as affirming God’s oneness and truth, and righteous action as performing God’s obligations and doing what is right in one’s relation to Him.
rows.anchor: {وآمن}: وحد الله وصدقه {وعمل صالحا}: أدى فرائض الله، وعمل صالحا فيما بينه وبين الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s report, ‘then was guided’ means recognizing that one’s guidance comes by God’s enabling.
rows.anchor: قال في رواية عطاء: (علم أن ذلك بتوفيق من الله له)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s report, ‘then was guided’ means that the person did not doubt.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الوالبي: (لم يشكك)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Abu Salih’s report, ‘then was guided’ means knowing one will be rewarded; Sufyan, al-Kalbi, al-Shaʿbi, and Muqatil share this view, and al-Zajjaj prefers it as persevering in faith.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية أبي صالح: (علم أن له ثوابا بهذا) (¬7)، هذا قول سفيان

rows.speaker: عطاء بن يسار
rows.claim: ʿAta ibn Yasar interprets guidance as following the Sunna in both word and deed.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء بن يسار: (ثم أصاب بقوله وعمله السنة)

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says guidance means holding to the Sunna and the community.
rows.anchor: وهذا نحو قول سعيد بن جبير: (لزم السنة والجماعة)

rows.speaker: فضيل الناجي
rows.claim: Al-Fudayl al-Naji glosses guidance as following the Sunna.
rows.anchor: وقال فضيل الناجي (¬3): (اتبع السنة)

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says guidance is knowledge that improves one’s practice; his son similarly says it is acting according to knowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: (علم علما يحسن به عمله. قال: يقول: {اهتدى} كيف يعمل)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says Moses hurried to God so that God’s satisfaction with him would increase; the author refers readers to his earlier discussion of ‘ulāʾ’ at 3:119.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (لتزداد رضا)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq explains that God put Israel into a trial and ordeal after Moses left.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أي ألقيناهم في فتنة ومحنة من بعدك)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says God made them wretchedly tested through calf worship, according to His prior decree, after Moses departed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: (صيرناهم مفتونين أشقياء بعبادة العجل لما سبق لهم في حكمنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Samiri was the means by which they went astray.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد أن الضلالة كانت على يدي السامري)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi explains that the Samiri led them to worship the calf.
rows.anchor: كما قال الكلبي: (فهم السامري إلى عبادة العجل)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a report through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abbas says the Samiri came from Bajarama to Egypt, joined Israel, came from a people who worshipped cattle, retained that devotion inwardly, and only outwardly professed Islam.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس: (كان السامري من أهل باجرمى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s report, Ibn Abbas identifies the Samiri as an Egyptian Copt, Moses’ neighbor, who believed and followed Moses but was then tested.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية عطاء: (كان السامري رجلا من القبط، جارا لموسى آمن به وصدقه وخرج معه فابتلي)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says most exegetes identify the Samiri as an Israelite notable from the Samira tribe, whose descendants still live in Syria as Samaritans.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (الأكثر في التفسير: أنه كان عظيما من عظماء بني إسرائيل من قبيلة تعرف بالسامرة

rows.speaker: راشد بن سعد
rows.claim: Rashid ibn Saʿd reports a dialogue in which God says Israel made a calf after Moses, Moses asks who gave it life, and God says He did; when Moses asks whether God misled them, God says He saw that inclination in their hearts and facilitated it.
rows.anchor: وروي عن راشد بن سعد (¬6) أنه قال: (قال الله لموسى: إن قومك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains that Israel already entertained anthropomorphic beliefs when they asked Moses for a god like other peoples’ gods; the calf trial repaid that belief and explains God’s saying that He saw it in their hearts and facilitated it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هذا أنهم كانوا يعتقدون التشبيه حين قالوا لموسى: {اجعل لنا إلها كما لهم آلهة}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAta’s report, Ibn Abbas says Moses asked who fashioned the calf’s body and gave it a sound; God answered that He did, and Moses swore that no one but God had led them astray, which God affirmed.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (قال موسى: يا رب هذا السامري أخرج لهم عجلا من حليهم، فمن جعل له الجسد والخوار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to his discussion in Sūrat al-Aʿraf for ‘angry and distressed.’
rows.anchor: سبق الكلام في هذا في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised good was the truthful promise to give Israel the Scripture.
rows.anchor: صدقا لإيتاء الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The long interval refers to the period Moses was away from them.
rows.anchor: {أفطال عليكم العهد} مدة مفارقتي إياكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about wanting God’s anger means their calf worship might cause His anger; no one seeks that anger directly, but may perform its cause.
rows.anchor: بعبادتكم العجل، وتلخيص المعنى: أم أردتم أن تصنعوا صنعا يكون سبب غضب ربكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Breaking Moses’ promise means failing to act as good successors after him, as also expressed at 7:150.
rows.anchor: ما وعدتموني من حسن الخلافة بعدي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets ‘you broke my promise’ as breaking the covenant and instruction Moses had given them to remain obedient to God.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ({فأخلفتم موعدي} قال عهدي)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interpretation that they failed to follow Moses’ path only works if Moses had promised them to do so; the author knows of no report that he made such a promise.
rows.anchor: وهذا إنما يصح لو روي أن موسى وعدهم ذلك، ولم نر في شيء من الروايات أن موسى وعد قومه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says they attributed breach to Moses’ promise to return to them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: ({فأخلفتم موعدي} أي: نسبتموه إلى الخلاف)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun ʿawaj has kasra for crookedness in religion, eyesight, and things that do not stand upright; with fatḥa it applies to a bent piece of wood.
rows.anchor: العوج: بكسر العين في الدين، وفي الطرف، وفيما لا ينتصب. والعوج: بالفتح في العود

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda defines amt as rises and dips, illustrating a rope or waterskin with no unevenness when stretched or filled.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: (الأمت: إرتفاع وهبوط، يقال: مد حبله حتى ما ترك فيه

rows.speaker: يزيد بن شيبة النميري
rows.claim: Yazid ibn Shayba al-Numayri’s poem describes a full-bodied woman as having no amt, supplying poetic evidence for the word’s use.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ليزيد بن شيبة النميري (¬1) (¬2): لها صورة كالشمس

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains bakhiya as full-bodied in form.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: (الباخية الممتلئة الخلق)

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says amt is the fold or sag in a waterskin that is not filled; when full, it has no amt.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: (الأمت: أن يصب في السقا ماء فلا يمتلئ فينثني

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra defines amt as a raised mound on the land and also describes a waterskin filled without unevenness.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: (الأمت موضع النبك

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrabi says amt is a hollow between raised places.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: (الأمت: وهدة بين نشوز)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s report, Ibn Abbas glosses ʿawaj as a valley and amt as a hill.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي: ({لا ترى فيها عوجا} يقول: واديا، {ولا أمتا} يقول: رابية)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets ʿawaj as a fissure and amt as a hill, agreeing with Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ({لا ترى فيها عوجا} أي: صدعا {ولا أمتا} ولا أكمة)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says ʿawaj means valleys and amt means mounds.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: ({لا ترى فيها عوجا} وهي الأودية {ولا أمتا} يعني النباك)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains that the land has neither a depression nor a rise.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: (لا انخفاضا ولا ارتفاعا)

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima reports from Ibn Abbas that there is neither a low nor a high place.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة عن ابن عباس: (ليس فيها منخفض ولا مرتفع)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Ibn al-Azraq’s report, Ibn Abbas defines amt as something protruding from the ground; in ʿAta’s report he calls it protuberances.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية بن الأزرق: (الأمت: الشيء الشاخص من الأرض)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says ʿawaj is a path among mountains and amt is a hillock.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (العوج: الطريق في الجبال، والأمت: الروابي)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that the exegetical and lexical opinions treat amt as a raised part of the ground.
rows.anchor: فهذه أقوال أهل اللغة والمفسرين في الأمت أنه: المرتفع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Hudhali reports al-Hasan’s distinction: ʿawaj is a low place and amt is raised ground.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو بكر الهذلي عن الحسن قال: (العوج: ما انخفض من الأرض، والأمت: ما نشز من الروابي)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the caller is heard as a voice calling people to the resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (صوت الداعي للحشر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exegetes identify the caller as God’s voice summoning people to the gathering place at resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: (يتبعون صوت داعي الله تعالى الذي يدعوهم إلى موقف القيامة)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says there is no turning away from the caller; the pronoun can refer to the caller or his voice, as in saying one cannot deviate from a summons.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (لا عوج لهم عن الداعي، وجاز أن يقول: {له}؛ لأن المذهب إلى الداعي وصوته

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says they cannot avoid following the caller.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (المعنى لا عوج لهم عن دعائه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says near and far are equal: everyone follows the voice and cannot turn away from it.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول ابن عباس: (يريد: البعيد والقريب سواء كلهم يتبع الصوت ولا يتعوج عنه)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s report, Ibn Abbas says the voices become still.
rows.anchor: قال الوالبي عنه: (يريد: سكنت)

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta says the voices are humbled and abased, as does al-Suddi.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: (يريد: خضعت وذلت)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining sound is the faintest sound, such as the whispering tread of feet.
rows.anchor: همس الأقدام أخفى ما يكون من الصوت

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says hams and rakz both mean a quiet sound; to whisper something is to conceal it in a low voice.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: (الهمس والركز واحد وهو: الصوت الخفي.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas cites a rajaz line about camels walking softly to illustrate the sound of their hoofs.
rows.anchor: وذكر عن ابن عباس أنه تمثل بقول الراجز (¬7): وهن يمشين بنا هميسا

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham says speech mouthed with closed lips is called hams and cites a line about eating provisions quietly.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الهيثم: (إذا مضغ

rows.speaker: أبو زبيد
rows.claim: Abu Zubayd’s line calls a lion hamūs because it walks stealthily in the dark.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول أبي زبيد (¬4) (¬5): فيأتوان يدلجون ويأت يسري

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In al-Walibi’s report, Ibn Abbas directly glosses hams as a faint sound.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية الوالبي في قوله: {إلا همسا} يقول: (الصوت الخفي)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In reports from Saʿid ibn Jubayr and ʿAta, Ibn Abbas specifies the sound as footsteps, like camels walking.
rows.anchor: وفسر ذلك الصوت في رواية سعيد بن جبير وعطاء فقال

rows.speaker: عكرمة، وسفيان، والحسن، والسدي
rows.claim: Most exegetes, including Ikrima, Sufyan, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi, interpret hams as the sound of feet moving toward the gathering; al-Farra and al-Zajjaj prefer this view.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول أكثر المفسرين قالوا: (يعني: صوت ثقل الأقدام إلى الحشر). وهذا قول عكرمة، وسفيان، والحسن والسدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Saʿid ibn Jubayr says Ibn Abbas interprets hams as lips moving without speech.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس {فلا تسمع إلا همسا}

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets hams as quiet speech.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد: (الكلام الخفي)
